name: Stripe
thesis: Stripe still sells the 2.9% + 30¢ it launched with in 2011. What changed is everything sold on top of it, and a consumer wallet that quietly makes leaving harder than arriving.

sections.title: Vitals
sections.summary: A private company with one audited window: its UK subsidiary.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.summary: In 2011, taking money online meant a merchant account, a gateway and a bank. Stripe made it seven lines of code.

sections.title: Users & Segments
sections.summary: Who Stripe says it serves, who says they left, and one team that wrote down why they came.

sections.title: Jobs To Be Done
sections.summary: Two jobs from the record: sell everywhere without a bank negotiation, and bill usage without building billing.

sections.title: The Product
sections.summary: One charge object, a wallet that follows the consumer, and a routing layer for platforms.

sections.title: Business Model
sections.summary: An unchanged headline rate, a growing stack priced on top, and reported cash flow that funds acquisitions.

sections.title: Growth Loops
sections.summary: Every link is documented. No link has an independent rate. Drawn open at one transition.

sections.title: Moats
sections.summary: One mechanism Stripe documents itself: credentials saved through Link do not leave.

sections.title: Bets & Tensions
sections.summary: A $53 billion bid that was withdrawn, and three bets still running: stablecoins, usage billing, agents.

sections.title: Verdict
sections.summary: Our call, with the ceiling stated.

problem.beforeState: As reported at launch in September 2011, a website that wanted to accept cards needed a merchant account and a payment gateway, negotiated with a bank, before it could take a single payment, and the card details passed through the developer's own servers. Stripe's founders described the prior arrangement as a finance problem that developers were being made to solve with finance tools.
problem.afterState: Stripe's stated proposition was that a developer could add card acceptance without a merchant account or gateway, at a published price of 2.9% plus 30 cents with no setup or monthly fees, with card data going straight to Stripe and payouts on a rolling seven-day basis. This is the launch proposition as contemporaneously reported, not a measurement of what changed for businesses.
problem.wedge: A payments API sold to the developer writing the checkout, priced per successful charge with no fixed fees, that removed the merchant-account prerequisite.

whyNow.change: By 2011 the person deciding how a web business took money was increasingly the developer building it, while incumbent processors still sold to finance departments through banks.
whyNow.argument: Stripe's founders framed the launch as enabling transactions being a problem rooted in code, not finance. Selling to the coder rather than the CFO is the wedge the 2011 coverage describes; whether the timing was demand-led or supply-led is not established by the record.

segments.name: Developer-led software businesses
segments.description: Startups and software companies whose engineers integrate Stripe directly, from the 2011 launch audience to the 2025 cohort Stripe describes as its fastest ever, 57% of it outside the US. The largest group by count on Stripe's own figures; its share of volume is not disclosed.

segments.name: Platforms and marketplaces
segments.description: Software platforms and marketplaces that use Connect to onboard their own sellers and route funds between parties. Stripe names Shopify, Airbnb, Lyft and DoorDash as examples in its documentation, and prices the segment separately per active account and per payout.

segments.name: Enterprises on negotiated terms
segments.description: Large companies Stripe says it serves across most of the Dow and Nasdaq 100, on custom pricing rather than the list rate. In the UK subsidiary, sales is the largest function by headcount, which points to a sold motion at the top of the market.

powerUser.profile: A global-by-default software business that runs Payments, Billing, Link and Atlas together and sells in more than a hundred countries from day one. Stripe's own account of Lovable fits this shape, and Apify's migration write-up describes a team that added Stripe for coverage and redundancy.
behaviours: Accepts payments from customers in 150 or more countries through one integration
Bills subscriptions and metered usage through Stripe Billing rather than in-house code
Sees a majority of checkouts arrive through Link-enrolled consumers
Incorporates through Atlas and takes a first payment within weeks

notFor.who: Businesses in categories Stripe restricts, or restricts later
notFor.why: One merchant describes its dating app being added to the Restricted Businesses list after two years on Stripe and losing its recurring subscriptions on closure. Stripe's export policy exists on paper; the account is about what happened in practice. One case, not a rate.

notFor.who: Small merchants whose volume suddenly jumps
notFor.why: Practitioner accounts describe reserves of 120 days or more triggered by transactions several times the usual size, with no phone support to resolve them. An inference from lived accounts; the same threads note that every online processor generates similar stories.

jobs.statement: When we sell software to customers in many countries, let us accept payment without negotiating a merchant account in each one.

competingAlternatives.name: A merchant account and gateway
competingAlternatives.why: The 2011 default: a bank relationship and a separate gateway before the first charge, with card data passing through the developer's servers.

competingAlternatives.name: Braintree
competingAlternatives.why: Apify chose Braintree first because it was the only major global provider supporting European companies at the time, and kept it running alongside Stripe after migrating.

forces.push: Coverage gaps and setup friction: a provider that did not support the company's country, or a bank process before the first sale.
forces.pull: One integration that accepts local payment methods in more than a hundred countries, priced per successful charge with no fixed fees.
forces.anxiety: Holds and closures without a person to call, documented by practitioners; and relying on one provider as a single point of failure, which Apify names as a reason to run two.
forces.habit: An existing processor integration and stored cards. Moving 10,000 users and 9,000 cards took Apify 18 working days.

jobs.statement: When our product charges by usage or seat, let us meter and invoice it without building a billing system ourselves.

competingAlternatives.name: In-house billing on top of raw payments
competingAlternatives.why: The default for a software team that already has Stripe payments: write the subscription, proration and retry logic itself.

competingAlternatives.name: Dedicated billing vendors
competingAlternatives.why: Practitioners list Chargebee, Chargify and open-source Lago among the alternatives; the trade is a second vendor against keeping billing next to the payment rail.

forces.push: Usage-based and hybrid pricing that in-house code handles badly: metering, proration, retries and invoices across currencies.
forces.pull: Billing models Stripe documents out of the box, plus Metronome for complex metering, on the same account as payments.
forces.anxiety: A further 0.7% of billing volume on top of processing, and subscriptions that Stripe does not export if the business ever leaves.
forces.habit: Existing subscription logic and customer records that would need remapping to move.

coreActions: Accept a payment through Checkout, Elements or the API
Recognise a returning consumer through Link and autofill their details
Route a payment to a connected account and take a platform fee
Bill a subscription or metered usage
Export saved cards to another processor
product.atomicUnitOfValue: A successful charge settled to the business's bank account, with no merchant account or gateway of its own.

keySurfaces.name: Dashboard
keySurfaces.purpose: The account, its balance, payouts, disputes and settings. Not observed; requires an account.

keySurfaces.name: Checkout
keySurfaces.purpose: Stripe-hosted payment page with Link, local payment methods and currency handling built in.

keySurfaces.name: Elements
keySurfaces.purpose: Embeddable payment components for a custom checkout, including the Payment Element and Express Checkout Element.

keySurfaces.name: Link
keySurfaces.purpose: Stripe's consumer wallet: saves and autofills payment and shipping details across businesses on Stripe.

keySurfaces.name: Connect
keySurfaces.purpose: Onboarding, payments and payouts for platforms and marketplaces with their own sellers.

keySurfaces.name: Billing
keySurfaces.purpose: Subscriptions, invoicing, quotes and usage-based billing, with Metronome for complex metering.

keySurfaces.name: Radar
keySurfaces.purpose: Fraud and abuse screening on every payment attempt, in four plans priced per screened transaction.

keySurfaces.name: Atlas
keySurfaces.purpose: Company incorporation in Delaware with a Stripe account attached.

businessModel.valueMetric: A percentage plus a fixed fee per successful charge, with each product sold on top priced as a further percentage of volume or a per-event fee.

revenueLines.name: Payment processing
revenueLines.description: The list rate of 2.9% + 30¢ on domestic US cards, unchanged since 2011, plus surcharges for international cards and currency conversion, plus Connect's per-account and per-payout fees. Independent reporting puts total 2024 revenue at $5.1 billion; Stripe discloses no split, so this line carries what the others do not.

revenueLines.name: Revenue suite: Billing, Invoicing, Tax, Metronome
revenueLines.description: Priced as a percentage of billed volume or a monthly plan. Stripe says the suite passed a $500 million run rate in 2024 and is on track for $1 billion during 2026, which against reported revenue makes it a significant but minority line.

revenueLines.name: Capital, Treasury, Issuing and interest
revenueLines.description: Capital is underwritten on Stripe data and funded by partner lenders; Issuing is in 22 countries; interest on customer balances is material at the UK entity level. Stripe's own 2024 words: Capital is not large today.

tiers.name: Pay as you go
gates: Self-serve signup, no setup or monthly fee

tiers.name: Products on top
gates: Billing 0.7% of billed volume or from $620 per month
tiers.priceNote: Each product a further percentage or per-event fee

tiers.name: Connect platforms
tiers.priceNote: Platform fees in addition to processing

tiers.name: Custom
gates: Negotiated rates for large payments volume or unusual business models
Interchange-plus and volume discounts not published

businessModel.monetizationMoment: The first successful charge in live mode. There is nothing to subscribe to, so Stripe's revenue starts with the business's own first sale and rises and falls with it; each product attached afterwards adds its own percentage to the same flow.
businessModel.unitEconomicsShape: Reported 2024 revenue of $5.1 billion against Stripe's stated $1.4 trillion of volume is a yield near 0.4%, well below the headline rate once interchange, enterprise discounts and platform pricing are netted, if both share a basis. Reported free cash flow of $2.2 billion, then about $3.2 billion, funds acquisitions from operations. Group margin is undisclosed.

brief.grows: A business signs up with no contract, and every payment leaves something behind: a consumer enrolled in Link, a data trail that underwrites Capital, volume that Billing and Radar attach to.
brief.earns: 2.9% + 30¢ per successful card charge, unchanged since 2011, plus surcharges and a stack of products each priced as a further slice of the same flow.
brief.tradeoff: It kept the headline price fixed and moved its pricing power into surcharges and add-ons, which are much harder for customers to compare.
brief.unverified: Stripe's group margin, and whether Link's non-portable credentials have ever cost a departing merchant anything real.

verdict.thesis: Stripe still sells the 2.9% + 30¢ it launched with in 2011. What changed is everything sold on top of it, and a consumer wallet that quietly makes leaving harder than arriving.

getRight.argument: 2.9% plus 30 cents at launch in 2011 and on the pricing page in 2026. The number merchants compare has stayed simple for fifteen years, which is a positioning asset in a category known for opaque pricing.

getRight.claim: Every new product sells to money already flowing
getRight.argument: Billing is priced on billed volume, Radar per screened transaction, and Capital is underwritten on the account's own processing history. Each is an upsell that needs no new customer.
The export page says card data is portable to any Level 1 processor and, on the same page, that Link credentials are not. Stating the asymmetry plainly is a trust asset most companies would not risk.

getWrong.claim: Support scales worse than the product
getWrong.argument: Practitioner accounts describe reserves of 120 days, closures without explanation, and no phone number to call. The self-serve funnel's failure mode lands on the smallest merchants, who have the least recourse.

getWrong.claim: Price changes that are hard to see
getWrong.argument: The international surcharge rose from 1.0% to 1.5%, the dispute fee stopped being refunded on won disputes, and the page announcing the European changes was later removed. A stable headline masks real movement.

getWrong.claim: A $53 billion bid, made in public and abandoned
getWrong.argument: Stripe and Advent walked away once PayPal's share price passed their offer. It revealed both an appetite for transformative deals and a price Stripe won't cross, and every future deal starts from that.

whatIdDoNext.move: Show every merchant their effective rate
whatIdDoNext.rationale: One dashboard figure for total fees as a share of volume, including surcharges and attached products, turns the least comparable part of the pricing into a signal of confidence.
whatIdDoNext.risk: Some merchants will see a number well above 2.9% and shop around, which is exactly what the current opacity prevents.

whatIdDoNext.move: Give every large hold a person and a date
whatIdDoNext.rationale: Any reserve above a threshold gets a named reviewer, a stated reason and a review date. The loudest criticism is about the absence of a person, not the existence of the hold.
whatIdDoNext.risk: It costs staff, and fraudsters will learn from the stated reasons.

whatIdDoNext.move: Measure Link's lift independently, then publish it
whatIdDoNext.rationale: If Link raises conversion for merchants who adopt Stripe, one independent study would turn Stripe's strongest asset from a claim into a selling point.
whatIdDoNext.risk: A small lift weakens the claim, and publishing it invites regulators to look at the credential-portability asymmetry.

openQuestions: What is Stripe's group margin, and on what revenue basis?
Has Link's non-portability ever cost a departing merchant a measurable share of its customers?
What happens to a business between its first charge and meaningful volume?
What did Bridge, Privy, Metronome and OpenRouter cost?
Does any agentic or stablecoin surface carry material volume yet?

interview.question: Stripe has charged 2.9% + 30¢ since 2011. How has it grown revenue per merchant without raising that price?
outline: Surcharges moved: international cards went from 1.0% to 1.5%, and won disputes stopped being refunded
New products are priced as slices of the same flow: Billing on volume, Radar per screen, Connect per account
Capital is underwritten on processing data the account already generates
The headline stays the comparison point, and the growth sits in everything around it

interview.question: Design a way to tell whether Link is really a moat.
outline: Define exposure: the share of a merchant's checkouts that use Link-saved credentials
Define the consequence to measure: the share of saved customers lost after migrating away
Say what data you need: merchants who left, with conversion before and after
Name the confound: Link also raises conversion, which is a reason to stay that has nothing to do with lock-in

interview.question: You own trust and safety for small merchants at Stripe. What do you change first?
outline: Name the failure mode: holds and closures with no person to talk to
Name who it hits: merchants with lumpy volume, and categories that get restricted later
Propose the fix: a named reviewer, a stated reason and a review date for large holds
Pick the metrics: time to resolution, churn after a hold, false-positive rate
State the trade-off: stated reasons teach fraudsters what gets flagged

interview.question: Why would Stripe bid $53 billion for PayPal, and what went wrong?
outline: Stripe stated no rationale; the reported enabler was about $3.2 billion of annual free cash flow
Strategic reads: PayPal's consumer wallet at scale against Link, branded checkout, Venmo
It failed because PayPal's share price rose past the bid once the interest leaked
The lesson: announcing interest moves the price you end up paying

patterns.note: Billing, Radar, Tax and Capital each add a percentage or a fee to payment volume that is already flowing.
Card data exports to any Level 1 processor; credentials saved through Link do not.
